hypothesis: The neuron responds strongly to prominent, high-contrast vertical or steeply diagonal linear features, typically manifesting as bright white or light gray bands, stripes, fissures, or elongated highlights set against a dark gray or black textured background. Specific activating examples include vertical white stripes on animal fur, bright metallic levers or handles, illuminated cracks between rock surfaces, and sharp linear highlights on beaks or claws. The neuron is invariant to the semantic identity of the subject (whether biological, geological, or manufactured), surface material, and lighting direction, provided the sharp light-on-dark (or occasionally dark-on-light) contrast and verticality are preserved. The activating linear feature typically spans 60–90% of the image height and is centered or positioned slightly off-center, occupying approximately 10–30% of the image width. The input images are consistently monochromatic, relying entirely on achromatic luminance contrast rather than chromatic hue.
